title: The Great Rotation: Why Wall Street's Chip Stocks Are Crashing While Banks and Energy Surge
excerpt: A punishing July selloff has wiped out gains in AI-related semiconductor stocks while overlooked sectors of the market quietly rally, reshaping the investment landscape.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The S&P 500 Momentum Index has dropped 10.6% from its June peak.
  • Semiconductor stocks fell over 13%, with Micron and SK Hynix down 25%.
  • Investors are shifting from AI tech to banks, energy, and retailers.
  • Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo view the market rotation as a healthy correction.
  • Over 69% of S&P 500 stocks are above their 200-day moving average.
  • The S&P 500 Momentum Index has fallen 10.6% from its June peak, entering correction territory after its strongest quarterly performance on record
  • Semiconductor stocks have dropped over 13% since late June, with Micron and SK Hynix losing 25% each, even as earnings reports came in strong
  • Banks, energy stocks and retailers are surging as investors rotate out of AI-heavy tech bets into old-economy sectors
  • Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo say the rotation is a "healthy reality check" — not a broad market selloff

Something unusual is happening beneath the surface of the U.S. stock market. While the headline indexes have wobbled only modestly in July, the internals tell a dramatically different story: the most popular trades of 2026 are unwinding at speed, and money is flowing into corners of the market that most investors had written off.

The Chip Trade Hits a Wall

The semiconductor sector, which powered the market's first-half rally on the back of artificial intelligence spending, has dropped more than 13% since its late June peak, according to data on the PHLX Semiconductor index. Micron Technology and South Korea's SK Hynix have each fallen roughly 25%.

What makes the selloff unusual is that the earnings news has been solid. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing raised its revenue forecasts, and ASML, the dominant chipmaking equipment maker, upgraded its 2026 outlook. Yet the stocks have not responded.

"If a company reports good earnings and the stock doesn't go up, it tells you everybody is in that trade."

— Stephanie Link, Chief Investment Strategist, Hightower Advisors

A high-beta momentum basket created by Goldman Sachs has fallen more than 30% from its peak. The 47 stocks in the Russell 1000 that had gained 100% or more during the first half of 2026 are now down an average of 21.6% since the start of July, according to Bespoke Investment Group.

Where the Money Is Going

The flip side of the chip rout is a broad rally in sectors that had lagged for months. Energy stocks, banks and retailers have all been trending higher. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF posted its biggest weekly outperformance versus the iShares Semiconductor ETF since May 2009, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

More than 69% of S&P 500 stocks were trading above their 200-day moving average last Thursday, the highest reading since late 2024. Market breadth, in other words, is improving — even as the biggest names stumble.

"The average stock is outperforming right now," said Adam Phillips, head of investments at EP Wealth. "Investors are just looking for something that seems a bit safer."

A Healthy Correction or the Start of Something Bigger?

Wall Street's major banks are framing the rotation as constructive rather than alarming. "The semiconductor and AI trade is undergoing a healthy reality check," said Darrell Cronk, CIO at Wells Fargo Investment Institute, though he cautioned that "the intermediate-term uptrend has been disrupted."

Morgan Stanley CIO Mike Wilson said the firm's "broadening thesis continues to play out" as former market leaders correct. This week's earnings from Alphabet, Tesla and Intel will be a crucial test of whether the tech selloff deepens or reverses.

Historical data offers some reassurance. Over the past 10 instances where the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF entered correction territory, the ETF rose an average of 12.4% over the following three months and 24% over the next year, with a roughly 90% win rate, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

What It Means for Indian Investors

The rotation carries direct implications for the Indian diaspora's U.S. portfolios. Many NRI investors are heavily exposed to technology-focused ETFs and semiconductor stocks through 401(k) plans and brokerage accounts. The shift toward banks, energy and consumer staples suggests diversification may be warranted.

The broader resilience of the market — with breadth improving rather than deteriorating — is a positive signal that the correction is orderly rather than systemic. But the speed of the rotation is a reminder that crowded trades can unwind quickly.
